meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Democracy is the theory that the common people know what they want, and deserve to get it good and hard'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified. Mencken printed it in The Smart Set, January 1915, p. 435, then collected it in A Little Book in C Major (1916). Public domain.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Mencken, and word for word. The sentence first appeared as §3 of the department “A Few Pages of Notes” in The Smart Set for January 1915, page 435 — printed under the headword “Vox Dei” and signed with the pen name William Drayham. Mencken collected it under his own name the following year in A Little Book in C Major (New York: John Lane Company, 1916). Both printings were read in the scanned originals.

A Little Book in C Major (New York: John Lane Company, 1916), page 19; later in A Mencken Chrestomathy (1949)
Exact. The familiar sentence is word-for-word what was printed; only the headword “Vox Dei” was dropped.

source.excerpt: Vox Dei—Democracy is the theory that the common people know what they want, and deserve to get it good and hard.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the sentence in a sourced section and cites “A Few Pages of Notes,” The Smart Set (January 1915), noting it was “later published in A Little Book in C major (1916), and A Mencken Crestomathy (1949).”

That citation checks out against the magazine itself. In the scanned January 1915 issue ↗, the department “A Few Pages of Notes” by William Drayham begins on page 435, and its §3 reads: “Vox Dei—Democracy is the theory that the common people know what they want, and deserve to get it good and hard.” The issue’s masthead names George Jean Nathan and H. L. Mencken as the editors.
William Drayham was Mencken’s own name in disguise: Wikipedia ↗ lists him among the pseudonyms Mencken published under, alongside Owen Hatteras and W.L.D. Bell.

The line then appears under Mencken’s own name in the facsimile of A Little Book in C Major ↗, whose title page reads “New York: John Lane Company, MCMXVI” with the notice “Copyright, 1916, by John Lane Company.”
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned issue. “Vox Dei” is the squib’s headword — a clipped nod to vox populi, vox Dei, “the voice of the people is the voice of God” — and it is the part everyone drops. Mencken dropped it himself when he reprinted the line in 1916.

author.name: H. L. Mencken
author.heading: The man who signed himself William Drayham
author.bio: Henry Louis Mencken (12 September 1880 – 29 January 1956) spent almost his entire working life at the Baltimore papers — The Sun, The Evening Sun and The Sunday Sun — while running a parallel career as America’s loudest and least reverent literary critic. In January 1915, the month this aphorism ran, he and George Jean Nathan were the named editors of The Smart Set; in 1924 the pair founded The American Mercury. He is remembered now for The American Language, his multi-volume study of how English is actually spoken in the United States, and for the savage dispatches from the Scopes “Monkey Trial” that he himself named.

misattribution.heading: What gets got wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is sound — this one really is Mencken, and the familiar wording is exactly his. What travels wrong is the paperwork, and the neighbouring Mencken lines people file next to it.

items.why: The standard citation stops at the book. Even Wikiquote’s Democracy page ↗ gives only “A Little Book in C Major (1916), p. 19.” The sentence had already run in The Smart Set in January 1915; Wikiquote’s own Mencken page ↗ carries the fuller chain.

The 1915 first printing carries no Mencken byline at all — the department is signed William Drayham, one of the pseudonyms Wikipedia lists for him ↗. Anyone searching the magazine for Mencken’s name will walk straight past page 435.

items.who: “No one ever went broke underestimating the intelligence of the American public”
items.why: Filed alongside this one as interchangeable Mencken-on-the-masses, but that line is corrupted. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to what Mencken actually printed in the Baltimore Evening Sun in 1926 — “No one in this world…has ever lost money by underestimating the intelligence of the great masses of the plain people” — with “lost money” later becoming “went broke” and “plain people” becoming “American public.” The democracy line, unusually, survived intact.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Mencken’s and it is exact: §3 of “A Few Pages of Notes,” The Smart Set, January 1915, page 435 ↗, reprinted in A Little Book in C Major the following year.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: This is not a considered thesis about self-government. It is one numbered squib in a run of them, wedged between a straight-faced defence of George Washington and a joke about polygamy, in a magazine Mencken was editing at the time. The whole charge sits in the last four words: strike “good and hard” and you are left with a mild compliment to the public’s judgment. Leave them in and the compliment becomes a sentence being passed.

The headword he printed above it — “Vox Dei” — is the joke made explicit. It clips the old tag vox populi, vox Dei, “the voice of the people is the voice of God,” and lets the aphorism supply the punchline. Almost nobody quoting the line today knows the headword was ever there; Mencken himself cut it when he reprinted the squib in book form the next year.
detailsBody: The department opens with §1, headed “The Light of Reason”: “An idealist is one who, on noticing that a rose smells better than a cabbage, concludes that it is also more nourishing.” That one is still in wide circulation too. §2 is a mock-defence of George Washington as a man who “had no faith in the infallible wisdom of the common people, and did his best to save the country from it” — the same thought as the democracy squib, stretched to a page.

When Mencken pulled the squibs into A Little Book in C Major the following year he stripped the headwords and resequenced them. In the book the democracy line comes first in the second part, directly after the section’s epigraph, and is followed by “Civilization is a concerted effort to remedy the blunders and check the practical joking of the Creator” and then the rose-and-cabbage idealist. Same material, no headwords, a different order — which is one reason the 1915 magazine printing is so easy to miss.
context.pull: “Vox Dei.” The headword he later cut is the whole joke.
